fields.title: Over 5200 cases recorded as Democratic Republic of the Congo crosses 100 days since Ebola outbreak declaration
fields.body:
\*\*Kinshasa—\*\*One hundred days have passed since the Democratic Republic of the Congo declared the ongoing Ebola outbreak, which has now become the country's fastest growing. Transmission is outpacing control efforts, requiring a substantial scale-up across all areas of response to halt the spread of the virus.

A daily average of around 90 confirmed cases has been recorded in the first three months, markedly higher than the rate observed in the same period during the 2014–2016 West Africa and the 2018–2020 Democratic Republic of the Congo outbreaks. The outbreak has now expanded to a sixth province, with Ituri remaining the epicentre, accounting for about 85% of cases and 79% of deaths.

“We can bring the Ebola outbreak under control but only through scaled-up action in affected communities that is led by national, provincial and local leaders and the affected communities, sustained by needed resources and backed by committed collaboration by all partners in DRC and beyond,” said Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, WHO Director-General. “WHO and partners will continue to support the DRC government, communities and neighbouring countries in delivering the response needed to end the outbreak.”

Mortality is high both in communities and among patients in treatment facilities. Community deaths—those occurring outside Ebola treatment centres—accounted for around 60% of the 260 weekly fatalities recorded over the past six weeks. This highlights the persistent challenges in early detection, referral and access to treatment, while mortality among patients reaching treatment facilities may reflect late admission and severe stage of the disease.

The response needs to be rapidly ramped up and adapted to local transmission patterns and operational gaps. All response partners need to reinforce operations in areas with high virus transmission and community deaths, as well as in high-risk areas and in areas reporting new cases. However, the response faces many challenges such as insecurity and recurrent conflict, population displacement, attacks on health facilities, community reluctance and difficult access. Scaling up and adapting the response requires intensified action and resource intense mobilization, stronger disease surveillance, preparedness and coordination across provinces, along the Congo River and national borders.

“This outbreak has reached a defining moment. The progress made over the past three months shows that stronger action delivers results, but it also reminds us that incremental gains will not be enough. We now need to significantly step up the response: moving faster to detect cases, reaching communities sooner and strengthening operations where they are needed most. The choices we make now will determine how quickly we can bring this outbreak under control, protect and save lives,” said Dr Mohamed Janabi, WHO Regional Director for Africa.

Despite the challenges, important outbreak response efforts have been made over the past three months. Laboratory capacity has expanded from one testing site to 19 laboratories capable of processing more than 3000 samples a day. Treatment capacity has increased from fewer than 10 beds to more than 1300, while over 900 health facilities have received infection prevention and control support. Community engagement activities have reached more than 2.5 million people and contact follow-up has improved from 9% during the first week of the outbreak to 84% as of 18 August.

Scientific efforts are also advancing, including clinical trials of potential treatments, evaluation of candidate vaccines and deployment of the first emergency-listed molecular diagnostic test for Bundibugyo virus disease. In countries neighbouring the Democratic Republic of the Congo and beyond, preparedness is being reinforced through closer cross-border collaboration, harmonized disease surveillance, information sharing and joint planning to detect and contain imported cases.

National authorities, supported by WHO and partners, are reinforcing disease surveillance and contact tracing, expanding laboratory testing and clinical care, strengthening infection prevention and control, and working with communities to encourage early reporting, care-seeking and safe and dignified burials. WHO has deployed over 260 experts, delivered more than 330 tonnes of essential medical and operational supplies.

Bringing the outbreak under control will require sustained national leadership, strong community engagement, secure access to affected communities, regional and global solidarity and continued investment to rapidly strengthen response operations where they are needed most. A halt in conflict is also critical to enable frontline teams to reach affected communities. The coming months will be critical to building on the gains made over the first 100 days, closing remaining operational gaps and accelerating efforts to contain the outbreak.

fields.title: DRC: The International Red Cross and Red Crescent Movement condemns attacks on its volunteers and staff | IFRC
fields.body:
**Kinshasa / Kampala / Geneva, 24 August 2026** - The Red Cross Societies of the Democratic Republic of the Congo (CRRDC) and Uganda (URCS), the International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies (IFRC), and the International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC) are deeply concerned about the attacks on Red Cross volunteers and staff in several incidents over the past few days.

One hundred days after the official declaration of the Ebola outbreak, 12 volunteers have been injured, ambulances have been damaged—including one that was set on fire—and emergency response equipment has been destroyed during 11 violent incidents.

On 19 August 2026, in Beni, North Kivu Province, three volunteers participating in humanitarian activities as part of the response to the Ebola virus disease were violently attacked and injured by a group of individuals. Equipment used in the response was also destroyed.

On 18 August 2026, two volunteers were also injured while attempting to conduct a safe and dignified burial in the village of Malikuti, in the Rungu health zone in Haut-Uélé. They were evacuated to Isiro to receive medical care following this incident, during which two vehicles were damaged.

Earlier, on 17 August 2026, a URCS convoy involved in the cross-border response was attacked in Aru, Ituri Province. One team member was seriously injured, and two ambulances belonging to the URCS were pelted with stones and vandalized.

Attacks against volunteers and humanitarian personnel are unacceptable. Respect for humanitarian personnel and humanitarian activities is essential to ensuring that communities affected by epidemics and other crises continue to receive the assistance and services they urgently need.

These attacks serve as an alarming reminder of the risks faced by humanitarian workers and volunteers engaged in the fight against epidemics and emergencies. Every personnel injured and every ambulance, vehicle, or piece of equipment damaged reduces the capacity to provide emergency health and humanitarian services, putting more lives at risk and making the epidemic harder to contain.

The CRRDC, the URCS, the ICRC, and the IFRC stand in solidarity with the injured volunteers and staff, their families, and all Red Cross personnel mobilized in the response. We wish the injured personnel a full and speedy recovery.

We call on communities, local leaders, and all relevant stakeholders to support, respect, and protect humanitarian action. Volunteers, health workers, and humanitarian staff must be able to carry out their work in complete safety, without fear of violence, intimidation, or threats.

The International Red Cross and Red Crescent Movement remains fully committed to supporting vulnerable communities in the Democratic Republic of the Congo and will continue its efforts to provide impartial humanitarian assistance to all those in need.

fields.title: RDC : Le Mouvement international de la Croix-Rouge et du Croissant-Rouge condamne les attaques contre son personnel | IFRC
fields.body:
**Kinshasa / Kampala / Genève, 24 août 2026** - Les Croix-Rouge de la République démocratique du Congo (CRRDC) et de l’Ouganda (URCS), la Fédération internationale des Sociétés de la Croix-Rouge (IFRC) et le Comité international de la Croix-Rouge (CICR) sont profondément préoccupés par les attaques dont ont été victimes des volontaires et staff de la Croix-Rouge lors de plusieurs incidents ces derniers jours.

Cent jours après la déclaration officielle de l'épidémie d'Ebola, 12 volontaires ont été blessés, des ambulances endommagées dont une incendiée et du matériel d’intervention détruit au cours de 11 incidents violents.

Le 19 août 2026, à Beni, dans la province du Nord-Kivu, trois volontaires qui participaient à des activités humanitaires dans le cadre de la riposte à la maladie à virus Ebola ont été violemment agressés et blessés par un groupe d'individus. Du matériel utilisé dans le cadre de l'intervention a aussi été détruit.

Le 18 août 2026, deux volontaires ont été également blessés pendant qu’ils tentaient d’effectuer un enterrement digne et sécurisé dans le village Malikuti, en zone de santé de Rungu dans le Haut-Uélé. Ils ont été évacués vers Isiro pour y recevoir des soins après cet incident, au cours duquel deux véhicules ont été endommagés.

Le 17 août 2026 déjà, un convoi de l’URCS intervenant dans le cadre de la riposte transfrontalière a été attaqué à Aru dans la Province de l’Ituri. Un membre de l’équipe a été gravement blessé et deux ambulances de la Croix-Rouge ougandaise caillassées et vandalisées.

Les attaques contre les volontaires et les intervenants humanitaires sont inacceptables. Le respect du personnel humanitaire et des activités humanitaires est essentiel pour garantir que les communautés touchées par les épidémies et d'autres crises continuent de recevoir l'assistance et les services dont elles ont urgemment besoin.

Ces attaques mettent en lumière, de manière alarmante, les risques auxquels sont exposés les travailleurs humanitaires et les volontaires engagés dans la lutte contre les épidémies et les situations d'urgence. Chaque volontaire ou staff blessé, et ambulance, véhicule ou équipement endommagé réduisent la capacité à fournir des services sanitaires et humanitaires d’urgence, ce qui met davantage de vies en danger et rend l’épidémie plus difficile à contenir.

La CRRDC, l’URCS, le CICR et l’IFCR expriment leur solidarité avec les volontaires et staff blessés, leurs familles ainsi qu'avec l'ensemble des équipes mobilisées dans la réponse. Nous adressons aux personnes blessées nos vœux de prompt et complet rétablissement.

Nous appelons les communautés, les leaders locaux et toutes les parties prenantes concernées à soutenir, respecter, et protéger l'action humanitaire. Les volontaires, les agents de santé et le personnel humanitaire doivent pouvoir accomplir leur mission en toute sécurité, sans crainte de violence, d'intimidation ou de menaces.

Le Mouvement international de la Croix-Rouge et du Croissant-Rouge demeure pleinement engagé aux côtés des communautés vulnérables en République démocratique du Congo et poursuivra ses efforts pour fournir une assistance humanitaire impartiale à toutes les personnes qui en ont besoin.

• According to WHO reporting as of 12 August 2026, active transmission has now been reported across five provinces in DRC: Ituri, North Kivu, Haut-Uélé, Tshopo, and South Kivu. WHO continues to characterize the outbreak as being in a phase of intense and expanding transmission.  
 • Insecurity, displacement, population movements and community resistance continue to complicate response efforts and increase the risk of further spread.  
 • The response is increasingly transitioning into a protracted emergency, with continued geographical expansion driving higher requirements for logistics, transport, storage and emergency telecommunications services.  
 • WHO and partners continue to expand treatment and operational capacity in eastern DRC, including additional Ebola Treatment Centres (ETCs) and Forward Logistics Bases (FLBs). The LTC remains ready to support increased requirements for cargo transport, storage, last-mile delivery and telecommunications services.  
 • Preparedness activities continued in South Sudan, Rwanda, Burundi, and CAR, focusing on cross-border readiness, pre-positioning of response assets, emergency telecommunications, logistics preparedness, and coordination along key mobility corridors.

fields.title: Termes de référence de la recherche : Étude de faisabilité des transferts monétaires 2026 (CAR2603) République centrafricaine, 01/08/2026 V1
fields.body:
**2. Justification**

**2.1. Contexte et informations générales**

La République centrafricaine (RCA) demeure confrontée à une crise humanitaire prolongée caractérisée par l'insécurité persistante, la pauvreté structurelle, les déplacements de population et une forte vulnérabilité aux chocs climatiques. Selon OCHA, 2,3 million de personnes, soit 36 % de la population, auront besoin d'une assistance humanitaire en 20261. Malgré certaines améliorations localisées, le pays reste parmi les plus pauvres du monde, avec environ 70 % de la population vivant sous le seuil international de pauvreté. La faiblesse des infrastructures, l'enclavement, la dépendance aux importations et les risques sécuritaires limitent fortement les capacités de résilience des ménages.

En 2026, les violences armées et les incidents affectant les acteurs humanitaires ont continué de limiter l'accès aux services essentiels et à l'aide, notamment à la suite de l'occupation d'Amdafoc par des groupes armés2 et de la suspension temporaire des activités humanitaires dans le Haut-Mbomou après l'assassinat d'un médiateur de paix3. Ces dynamiques ont alimenté des mouvements importants de population: à la fin de l'année 2025, la RCA comptait plus de 428 000 personnes déplacées internes, tandis que près de 665 000 réfugiés centrafricains vivaient encore dans les pays voisins.

Parallèlement, l'insécurité alimentaire reste préoccupante. Selon l'IPC, près de 1,92 million de personnes étaient en situation d'insécurité alimentaire aiguë entre septembre 2025 et mars 2026, un chiffre susceptible d'atteindre 2,3 millions durant la période de soudure de 20264.

Dans ce contexte, les transferts monétaires et les coupons constituent une modalité d'assistance essentielle pour répondre de manière flexible et digne aux besoins des populations affectées. Toutefois, leur mise en œuvre dépend de plusieurs facteurs, notamment la fonctionnalité des marchés, l'accès aux biens et services, la disponibilité des prestataires financiers et les risques de protection.

À ce jour, les informations disponibles sur la faisabilité des transferts monétaires en RCA restent fragmentées: elles proviennent d'évaluations ponctuelles menées par différentes agences dans le cadre de projets spécifiques, sans cadre d'analyse commun ni couverture harmonisée des sous-préfectures prioritaires. Le JMMI et le MSNA fournissent des données récurrentes sur les marchés et les ménages, mais aucune analyse consolidée ne croise à ce jour ces sources avec les capacités des prestataires de services financiers et des acteurs humanitaires, pourtant déterminantes pour juger de la faisabilité opérationnelle du cash. Cette absence de vision partagée expose les acteurs du GTC à des évaluations parallèles, redondantes ou peu comparables entre agences, ce qui complique la prise de décision collective sur les modalités d'assistance à privilégier selon les zones. Combler cette lacune est d'autant plus urgent que le cycle de planification HPC 2027 approche et nécessitera des bases analytiques robustes et partagées entre partenaires.

Plusieurs sous-préfectures ont été priorisées dans le cadre du HNRP 2026, nécessitant une analyse commune de faisabilité cash afin d'identifier les zones où cette modalité est appropriée et les conditions de sa mise en œuvre. Cette évaluation vient directement appuyer les efforts déjà engagés par le Groupe de Travail Cash pour harmoniser les approches CVA en RCA et réduire la duplication des évaluations entre agences. Ses résultats alimenteront directement la préparation du prochain cycle de planification humanitaire (HPC), en fournissant aux acteurs humanitaires une base analytique commune sur laquelle fonder leurs décisions d'allocation. L'analyse contribuera également à soutenir les échanges avec les bailleurs de fonds, en démontrant que les interventions cash proposées reposent sur une évaluation structurée des marchés, des risques et des capacités opérationnelles. L'initiative sera menée dans une approche inter-agences, sous la coordination du Groupe de Travail Cash, avec l'appui d'IMPACT/REACH, du PAM et de Hulo.

fields.title: Rapport de la situation epidemiologique du cholera en RD Congo (Interne OMS), semaine 32, 2026
fields.body:
**I. POINTS SAILLANTS**

• Le nombre de cas suspects de choléra notifiés SE32 (1 528) est de l’ordre de celui rapporté SE31 qui représentait une forte augmentation

• A la 32 ème semaine épidémiologique, le nombre de cas suspects notifiés reste largement supérieur au seuil de 1 000 cas suspects de choléra, comme depuis plusieurs semaines. Ce niveau d’incidence est alarmant à l’approche de la saison des pluies.

• À la 32ème semaine épidémiologique, 16 sur 26 provinces ont notifié des cas suspects de choléra dans 70 zones de santé sur les 519 que compte le pays.

• Aucune zone de santé nouvellement affectée à la 32 ème semaine épidémiologique sur l’ensemble du territoire sanitaire de la RD Congo. • A la 32ème semaine épidémiologique, les provinces du Sud-Kivu et du Nord-Kivu, seules ont notifié plus de la moitié soit (52,55 %) des cas suspects de choléra.

• Préparatifs de la vaccination anticholérique orale préventive dans les ZS de Mulungu et Shabunda (DPS Sud-Kivu) à la mi-septembre, avec sensibilisation communautaire et attente de l’approbation du financement.

• Dans la DPS du Nord-Kivu, affrontements armés dans 5 ZS hotspots avec déplacements massifs de populations et accès limité aux zones affectées, aggravés par des conditions d’hygiène et sanitaires précaires dans les aires de santé de retour de Masisi.

• Les préparatifs de la campagne VCO dans les îlots du corridor du fleuve Congo se poursuivent, avec un plan conjoint de vaccination transfrontalière RDC–République du Congo élaboré avec l'appui de l'OMS.

fields.title: Cameroon Humanitarian Update - August 2026
fields.body:
**National Humanitarian Forum seeks strategic alignment as Cameroon’s humanitarian transition advances**

The National Humanitarian Forum took place in Yaounde on 26 May 2026, bringing together more than 140 participants from government, national and international NGOs, the United Nations, donors, technical and financial partners, and the media. The forum aimed to foster strategic alignment among humanitarian, development and government actors on the humanitarian situation, the ongoing humanitarian transition, the localization of aid, and financing and accountability issues.

Opening the forum, the UN Resident Coordinator and Humanitarian Coordinator (RC/HC), Issa Sanogo said collaboration between national and local authorities, humanitarian partners and donors delivered life-saving assistance to one million people in 2025. He noted a persistent gap: only half of the 2.1 million people targeted were reached, leaving 1.1 million people without support. He linked the forum to the Humanitarian Reset, the global reform under which Cameroon is one of eight countries selected by the Inter-Agency Standing Committee (IASC) to shift toward a more localized, nationally led coordination model.

The Director of Civil Protection (DPC) at the Ministry of Territorial Administration (MINAT), Angele Ndzie Ntsama, welcomed continued partner support and committed the Government to strengthening coordination, consultation and response mechanism. She called for collective reflection on the role of national and local actors, accountability to affected populations, and stronger links between humanitarian action, development and peacebuilding.

Panel discussions confirmed that Area-Based Coordination (ABC) is now operational in the Far North, North-West and South-West regions at a regional level and in some divisions. Under the Civil Protection Law of 23 December 2024, MINAT/DPC holds legal responsibility for coordinating the humanitarian response. Hundreds of national NGOs are still active in the Far North, North-West and South-West coordination platforms, and the Lake Chad Basin Nexus Facility Fund, which reserves 30 per cent of its financing for local actors, has already supported two consortia in Cameroon and Chad.

Recommendations from the forum called for international financing and government contributions to be presented jointly for a transparent view of resources, for responsibilities to transfer together with corresponding human, logistical and budgetary means, and for a dedicated donor meeting to align financing mechanisms behind the transition.

Closing the forum, the RC/HC reiterated that the transition is not a disengagement but an accompanied, responsible transfer of responsibility, and reaffirmed the commitment of the United Nations and humanitarian partners to mobilize funding so that no vulnerable community is left without support. The Directorate of Civil Protection reaffirmed the Government’s commitment to strengthened national coordination and accountability.

(N'Djamena, 20 août 2026) – Le Coordonnateur des secours d'urgence des Nations Unies a alloué 4 millions USD du Fonds central d'intervention pour les urgences humanitaires (CERF) pour**7 millions USD pour répondre aux nouveaux déplacements et à l'épidémie de choléra dans la province du Lac** répondre aux urgences dans la province du Lac. Cette allocation vient compléter 3 millions USD du Fonds humanitaire régional pour l’Afrique de l’Ouest et du Centre (FHRAOC), déboursés par le Coordonnateur humanitaire. Ces 7 millions permettront aux partenaires humanitaires de répondre aux nouveaux déplacements de population enregistrés en juin ainsi qu’à l’épidémie de choléra, apparue début août.

En effet, les violences provoquées par les groupes armés non-étatiques (GANE) ont contraint plus de 75 210 personnes à fuir leurs localités d'origine vers 16 sites répartis dans les sous-préfectures de Baga-Sola, Daboua, Kaiga-Kindjiria, Liwa et Ngouboua. Ces populations sont arrivées démunies, dans des zones où les services de base étaient déjà saturés par la présence de déplacés antérieurs, de retournés et de communautés hôtes elles-mêmes vulnérables.

A cette crise de déplacement s'est ajoutée l’épidémie de choléra, confirmée à Kangalom le 6 août. Selon le rapport de situation n°35 du ministère de la Santé publique, la province du Lac a enregistré, au 16 août, 219 cas et 8 décès, répartis sur les districts sanitaires de Bol, de Kangalom, de Bagassola et de Liwa. La promiscuité sur les sites, l'accès limité à l'eau potable et à l'assainissement et la mobilité des populations autour du lac créent des conditions propices à une propagation rapide de l’épidémie.

**Une réponse répartie entre trois enveloppes complémentaires**

Sur les 4 millions USD du CERF, 3 millions sont consacrés à la réponse aux nouveaux déplacements, notamment dans les secteurs de la santé, de la nutrition et de la protection. Mis en œuvre par l’OMS, l’UNICEF et l’UNFPA, ces fonds permettront d’assurer les soins essentiels de santé d’urgence, la prise en charge de la malnutrition aiguë, le soutien aux survivantes de violences basées sur le genre et la protection des enfants séparés ou non accompagnés.

Le million de dollars restant a été débloqué en urgence pour la riposte à l’épidémie de choléra, à parts égales entre l’OMS et l’UNICEF. Cette enveloppe couvre les secteurs de la santé et de l'eau, hygiène et assainissement. Elle permettra de renforcer la prise en charge des cas dans les unités et centres de traitement du choléra, la surveillance épidémiologique à base communautaire, la désinfection des habitations et des centres de traitement, la chloration des points d'eau et la communication sur les risques, dont les outils faisaient jusqu'ici défaut dans la province.

Les 3 millions de dollars du FHRAOC complètent ce dispositif sur les secteurs des abris et articles ménagers essentiels, de l'eau, hygiène et assainissement et de l'assistance alimentaire. Cette répartition a été construite pour éviter tout chevauchement entre les deux fonds, chacun couvrant des secteurs/actions distincts au bénéfice des mêmes populations.

*« Ces financements arrivent au moment où deux urgences se superposent dans le Lac : le déplacement de populations et l'épidémie de choléra. Les fonds ne couvrent pas l'ensemble des besoins, mais ils permettent d'agir vite et de confier une part significative de cette réponse aux organisations tchadiennes qui sont déjà sur les sites »,* a déclaré Dr François Batalingaya, Coordonnateur humanitaire pour le Tchad.

**Une réponse conduite au plus près du terrain**

L'allocation du FHRAOC accorde une place déterminante aux organisations nationales. Une part importante de l'enveloppe est attribuée directement à des ONG nationales, retenues pour leur ancrage territorial dans le Lac, leur capacité opérationnelle et leur accès aux zones insulaires difficilement atteignables par les acteurs internationaux. Ce choix prolonge l'orientation prise par le Fonds au Tchad.

Le plan intersectoriel de réponse aux nouveaux déplacements dans le Lac requiert 15,12 millions USD (juillet-décembre 2026), tandis que la riposte au choléra est estimée à 2,34 millions USD (juillet-septembre 2026). Les 7 millions USD mobilisés couvrent une part importante des besoins, mais des financements complémentaires restent nécessaires. Un plaidoyer est en cours auprès des bailleurs, alors que le Plan de réponse humanitaire 2026 du Tchad n’est financé qu’à 35 % des 986,1 millions USD requis.

fields.title: IOM: Multi-Country Bundibugyo Ebola Virus Disease Outbreak - Situation Report No. 14 (10-16 August 2026)
fields.body:
**SITUATION OVERVIEW**

According to the World Health Organization, as of 16 August, the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) reported 5,001 confirmed cases of Ebola disease caused by the Bundibugyo virus (BVD), including 2,378 deaths.

With the recent increase in figures, the Ebola Bundibugyo outbreak has become the largest and fastest-growing outbreak in DRC. The rapidly escalating outbreak is unfolding against the backdrop of an ongoing triple crisis in eastern DRC, where health risks, largescale displacement and persistent conflict intersect. Given the high case fatality rate of 81% in internally displaced persons (IDP) sites, as per WHO and Africa CDC, a multisectoral response to multidimensional needs of displaced populations is critically required.

The spread of the outbreak into Bas-Uélé Province underscores the continued need to comprehensively address the mobility dimensions of the ongoing public health response. Community deaths account for over 50 per cent of fatalities as per government sources, indicating ongoing gaps in case detection and health-care seeking. Contact tracing is particularly weak in Bas-Uélé (18.9%), highlighting the need for continued disease surveillance and monitoring to ensure a complete epidemiological picture.

The rapid geographic expansion of the outbreak creates additional needs for hygiene supplies, infection prevention and control (IPC) consumables and health infrastructure, such as ambulances, to support timely prevention, detection, referral and response. In parallel, the rising number of cases in Haut-Uélé requires enhanced disease surveillance and cross-border coordination to prevent disease transmission into neighbouring South Sudan and the Central African Republic (CAR).

Cross-border movements, displacement and population mobility continue to shape disease transmission, requiring an urgent and rapid response to save lives and protect people in affected areas, while mitigating regional health risks. Given the rapidly escalating crisis, IOM’s preparedness and response efforts aim to enhance monitoring at points of entry (PoEs) and points of control (PoCs), particularly along the Congo River, to strengthen detection and response capacities.

In line with the Inter-Agency Standing Committee (IASC) systemwide scale-up activation for infectious disease events, IOM has scaled up its response, enabling enhanced surge support, operational capacity and coordination across affected countries.

IOM’s response continues to focus on Priority 1a countries, DRC and Uganda, where outbreak response and enhanced preparedness activities remain ongoing, and Priority 1b countries, Burundi, Rwanda and South Sudan, which face an elevated risk of crossborder transmission. Preparedness interventions are also being implemented in other at-risk countries across the region, including Priority 2 countries, Angola, CAR, Ethiopia, Kenya, the Republic of the Congo, the United Republic of Tanzania and Zambia, to strengthen readiness and enhance regional health security, while supporting continent-wide efforts, particularly as co-lead of the PoE technical working group at the continental level.

fields.title: Cameroon | Floods in Fako DREF Operation No.: MDRCM045
fields.body:
**Date of event** 05-08-2026

**What happened, where and when?**

In the early hours of Wednesday, August 5, 2026, after more than a month of continuous rains, torrential downpours fell on the coastal city of Limbe, in the department of Fako, South-West region of Cameroon. At around 6:30 a.m., the waterlogged hillside overlooking the Mbende and Gardens neighborhoods gave way. The landslide swept away an inhabited house, burying its four sleeping occupants. Three adult women died, including a pregnant woman who lost her unborn child. The fourth occupant, an adult male, was pulled alive from the rubble by Cameroon Red Cross volunteers and community members. He is currently hospitalized in intensive care at the regional hospital of Limbe. The lives of many people are threatened and the search continues.

These same rains saturated the drainage systems of Limbe and Jenguele. Runoff from the Mount Cameroon massif carried mud, rocks, vegetation and solid waste accumulated in the residential plain, flooding Down Beach, Church Street, Motowoh, Mawoh, Mabeta New Layout, Cité SIC, Isokolo, Manga Williams Avenue, Bonjo and the Mile 1, 2 and 4 districts. The fence of the Limbé Wildlife Centre has been breached. Water entered the offices of the Bank of Central African States (BEAC), an unprecedented event in the city's institutional memory. Roads have become impassable for pedestrians and vehicles. Cassava fields and markets have been flooded, with significant losses of goods.

As of August 8, 2026, several neighborhoods remain under water. More than 1,500 households, or about 12,000 people, are affected, and nearly 2,000 people (250 households) whose homes were completely flooded are now homeless and in an emergency situation. The fairly large number of people with special needs remains very worrying, with nearly 700 people concerned.

Stagnant water, contaminated with faeces, accumulates in low-lying and densely populated neighbourhoods, where shallow wells are the main source of drinking water, in a region which has repeatedly been the epicenter of national cholera outbreaks.

The Fako Departmental Committee in Limbe, in collaboration with the prefect of Fako, the mayor and the security forces, continues to assess the situation as it evolves. The departmental committee, which does not have a contingency stock, is almost powerless in the face of the situation, which continues to grow. If nothing is done in the coming days, the humanitarian situation in the city of Limbe could spiral out of control.

fields.title: 100 days of Ebola disease outbreak: Faster and more flexible response needed to curb deadly spread in DRC
fields.body:
As it approaches 100 days since the [Ebola disease outbreak](https://www.msf.org/drc-ebola-outbreaks) was declared in [Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC)](https://www.msf.org/democratic-republic-congo-drc), Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF) warns that communities are not receiving adequate support to contain the disease. This [outbreak](https://www.msf.org/epidemics-and-pandemics) has become the largest and deadliest in the country’s history, and it continues to spread at an alarming rate within communities who already contend with [conflict](https://www.msf.org/war-and-conflict), violence, [displacement](https://www.msf.org/refugees-idps-and-people-move), and hunger, among other health emergencies, in their daily lives.  
  
Training for health workers and community leaders on case detection, referrals, and infection prevention and control measures must be urgently bolstered within communities affected by the outbreak.  
  
Over the past week, deaths due to [Ebola disease](https://www.msf.org/ebola) have been reported at a rate of roughly one every half hour. Since the outbreak began and as of 16 August, national authorities have reported more than 5,000 confirmed cases and over 2,400 deaths.   
  
“This epidemic continues to spread, moving faster than the response can keep up,” says Dr Javid Abdelmoneim, International President of MSF. “Treatment centres remain essential for saving lives, but this response needs more than extra beds.”

“It needs better detection, safe isolation for sick people and their contacts, and support to health workers,” says Dr Abdelmoneim. “People seeking care in existing health facilities also need to be protected from infection. Crucially, the response must be built *with* communities, not around them.”  
  
In Rho displacement camp, near Drodro, Ituri province, community leaders have worked with MSF to encourage people with symptoms to seek testing, isolation and treatment early. They also promote infection prevention and control measures to reduce the risk of community transmission. In the overcrowded camp, which is home to nearly 50,000 people, this collaboration has helped limit the spread of Ebola and reduce mortality.  
  
“We know our communities and how to reach our people,” says Ezrome Kiza Lumani, a community leader living in the camp. “When Ebola arrived, we did not wait. We spoke with families, listened to their fears, and encouraged people with symptoms to seek care. We have a crucial role to play in stopping this outbreak.”  
  
Since the outbreak was officially declared, more than 60 per cent of Ebola disease deaths in DRC have occurred outside – and often far away from – Ebola treatment centres. This means many people are dying at home or in their communities without receiving care, and the virus continues to spread before cases are detected.  
  
Worryingly, case numbers are rising rapidly beyond the epicentre of Ituri, with North Kivu province experiencing particularly high levels of mortality and mistrust in the response.

  
“With cases emerging in new areas with little or no previous experience managing Ebola disease, Ebola-trained healthcare workers are urgently needed not only inside treatment centres, but also directly in affected communities,” says Trish Newport, MSF’s emergency programme manager in Ituri.  
  
MSF is currently responding across Ituri, North Kivu, South Kivu, Tshopo, and Haut-Uélé provinces. Teams are operating six Ebola treatment centres, as well as isolation units, in affected areas, with more than 400 beds available — representing one third of all beds in the overall response. More than 1,400 MSF staff are supporting the response. Since the start of the outbreak, our teams have admitted more than 2,000 patients, of which more than 800 patients were confirmed to have Ebola disease.  
  
In Beni, North Kivu province, we have worked to move our response within communities. Through supporting existing health facilities that also offer general healthcare services, which are also crucial to saving lives, systematic and symptomatic treatment can start quickly. Across the response to the outbreak in DRC, more must be done to ensure people can receive the care they need closer to home.  
  
“Health workers and community leaders need training to help detect cases early, refer people safely, reinforce infection prevention and control, and protect themselves and others from infection,” says Newport. “The World Health Organization (WHO), other UN agencies, humanitarian organisations, including MSF, and the Congolese Ministry of Health must urgently expand this training and support.”

Community leaders like Emery Guba Mateso, also from Rho displacement camp, are sharing their experiences to encourage people to seek care. He lost his son to the disease and later survived an infection himself.  
  
“As a person who has recovered from Ebola disease, the message I would like to share with the community is: as soon as the first symptoms appear, it is important to seek medical care promptly, because early access to appropriate treatment increases the chances of recovery,” says Guba Mateso.

fields.title: Ebola-Related Incident Analysis - CPT Signals and Implications - July 2026
fields.body:
This incident analysis, covering the period from 2 to 31 July 2026, points to an acceleration and, above all, a transformation in the nature of the risk surrounding the response. A total of 97 incidents were recorded over 30 days, compared with 68 over the 47 days of the previous period. While the average severity of incidents is falling in terms of casualties, their frequency is rising sharply and their geographical spread is widening. Ituri remains the province most affected, but North Kivu now accounts for a far larger share of incidents, while Tshopo and Haut-Uélé have entered our monitoring.

Beyond this quantitative increase, three distinct — though at times interlocking — risk systems now shape the operational environment of the response. The first remains community friction, chiefly around safe and dignified burials, prevention activities and health facilities. It is, however, shifting towards North Kivu, with Beni and Butembo among the main flashpoints. The second is contestation internal to the response, linked in particular to arrears in incentive payments, salaries and other payments, and especially visible in Bunia and Rwampara, where staff protests have disrupted the functioning of health facilities and certain response activities. The third arises from territorial control exercised by armed actors, some of whom are appropriating or instrumentalising public health measures, notably in Lubero and Irumu.

This shift is accompanied by a change in the forms confrontation takes. Ebola treatment centres (ETCs), isolation centres and other health facilities are increasingly becoming targets in their own right. The emergence of threats made conditional on the notification of new cases, documented in particular in Biena, Musienene and Beni, is a particularly worrying signal: it may now affect not only the security and acceptance of the response, but also case notification and, consequently, the quality of epidemiological surveillance. The Nyakunde sequence further illustrates how quickly a grievance relating to patient care can escalate into community mobilisation, armed intervention and an interruption of the response.

The geography of priorities has also been profoundly redrawn. Beni and Butembo have become critical flashpoints in North Kivu, while Nyakunde has emerged as a major new rupture zone in Ituri. Bunia and Rwampara remain priorities, but their profile is shifting towards a crisis bound up with the internal functioning of the response rather than with community acceptance alone. Conversely, the absence of recorded incidents in Mongbwalu, previously one of the main hotspots, must be interpreted with caution until genuine de-escalation has been distinguished from a possible breakdown in reporting.

These developments make a uniform response focused exclusively on risk communication and community engagement (RCCE) inadequate. They call for a differentiated approach combining mediation and community engagement in areas of resistance, rapid resolution of contractual and financial grievances within the response, physical protection of health facilities, and access negotiation in spaces under the influence of armed groups. For the month of August, particular attention will need to be paid to resolving the incentive payments crisis, to the spread of conditional threats, to the instrumentalisation of public health measures by armed actors, to developments in the new flashpoints in Tshopo and Haut-Uélé, and to the situation in Mongbwalu.

fields.title: Analyse d’incidents liés à Ebola - Signaux CPT et implications - juillet 2026
fields.body:
Cette analyse d’incidents couvrant la période du 2 au 31 juillet 2026 met en évidence une accélération et, surtout, une transformation de la nature du risque entourant la riposte. Au total, 97 incidents ont été recensés en 30 jours, contre 68 au cours des 47 jours de la période précédente. Si la gravité moyenne des incidents diminue en termes de victimes, leur fréquence augmente fortement et leur géographie s’élargit. L’Ituri demeure la principale province concernée, mais le Nord-Kivu représente désormais une part beaucoup plus importante des incidents, tandis que la Tshopo et le Haut-Uélé apparaissent dans notre suivi.

Au-delà de cette progression quantitative, trois systèmes de risque distincts mais parfois imbriqués structurent désormais l’environnement opérationnel de la riposte. Le premier reste une friction communautaire, principalement autour des enterrements dignes et sécurisés, des activités de prévention et des structures de santé. Elle se déplace toutefois vers le Nord-Kivu, avec Beni et Butembo parmi les principaux foyers. Le deuxième est une contestation interne à la riposte, liée notamment aux arriérés de primes, de salaires et de paiements, particulièrement visible à Bunia et Rwampara, où les mouvements d’agents ont perturbé le fonctionnement de structures sanitaires et certaines activités de réponse. Le troisième relève du contrôle territorial exercé par des acteurs armés, certains s’appropriant ou instrumentalisant les mesures sanitaires, notamment dans le Lubero et l’Irumu.

Cette évolution s’accompagne d’un changement dans les formes de confrontation. Les centres de traitement Ebola (CTE), centres d’isolement et autres structures sanitaires deviennent davantage des cibles en tant que telles. L’apparition de menaces conditionnées à la déclaration de nouveaux cas, documentées notamment à Biena, Musienene et Beni, constitue un signal particulièrement préoccupant : elle peut désormais affecter non seulement la sécurité et l’acceptation de la riposte, mais également la déclaration des cas et, par conséquent, la qualité de la surveillance épidémiologique. La séquence de Nyakunde illustre par ailleurs la rapidité avec laquelle un grief lié à la prise en charge peut évoluer vers une mobilisation communautaire, une intervention armée et une interruption de la réponse.

La géographie des priorités s’est également profondément renouvelée. Beni et Butembo deviennent des foyers critiques au Nord-Kivu, tandis que Nyakunde apparaît comme une nouvelle zone de rupture majeure en Ituri. Bunia et Rwampara restent prioritaires, mais leur profil évolue vers une crise davantage liée au fonctionnement interne de la riposte qu’à la seule acceptation communautaire. À l’inverse, l’absence d’incidents enregistrés à Mongbwalu, auparavant l’un des principaux hotspots, doit être interprétée avec prudence tant qu’une désescalade réelle n’a pas été distinguée d’une éventuelle faiblesse de la remontée d’information.

Ces évolutions rendent inadaptée une réponse uniforme centrée exclusivement sur la communication des risques et engagement communautaire (CREC/RCCE). Elles appellent une approche différenciée combinant médiation et engagement communautaire dans les zones de résistance, résolution rapide des griefs contractuels et financiers au sein de la riposte, sécurisation des structures de santé, et négociation d’accès dans les espaces sous influence des groupes armés. Pour le mois d’août, une attention particulière devra être portée à la résolution de la crise des primes, à l’extension des menaces conditionnelles, à l’instrumentalisation des mesures sanitaires par les acteurs armés, à l’évolution des nouveaux foyers en Tshopo et au Haut-Uélé, ainsi qu’à la situation de Mongbwalu.

fields.title: WFP Central African Republic Country Brief, August 2026
fields.body:
**KEY HIGHLIGHTS**

• The updated March 2026 IPC analysis for AprilAugust 2026 projects that over 2 million people will face acute food insecurity, underscoring the need for sustained assistance throughout the lean season.

• WFP provided food and cash assistance to more than 62,000 vulnerable people, contributing to the stabilization of household food consumption, amid rising prices and deteriorating economic access to food.

• Despite insecurity and access constraints in the north-east, WFP continues to deliver an integrated response combining emergency assistance, nutrition support, school feeding, resiliencebuilding activities and critical supply chain services.

**SITUATION OVERVIEW**

• The Central African Republic faces protracted insecurity, regional spillover from Sudan and sustained displacement. Over 2 million people are projected to face acute food insecurity (IPC Phase 3+) between April and August 2026, including 262,000 people in Emergency (IPC Phase 4). Refugees, IDPs, returnees and host communities remain among the most affected populations, while access constraints persist in border areas such as Vakaga.

• Humanitarian needs remain high during the peak of the lean season, while food assistance is constrained by limited funding. Market monitoring indicates increasing pressure on household economic access to food, with elevated food basket costs and localized shortages of staple commodities reported in several hard-to-reach areas.

• Operational capacity and humanitarian access remain constrained by insecurity, logistical challenges and reduced funding for common services. Insecurity in north-eastern areas, particularly around Birao, together with seasonal road access constraints, continued to affect the movement of humanitarian supplies and the delivery of assistance.

• While no Ebola cases have been confirmed incountry, WFP is supporting government-led preparedness efforts to the ongoing outbreak in neighbouring Democratic Republic of the Congo.

fields.title: Central African Republic: Situation Report No. 81, as of 18 August 2026
fields.body:
**HIGHLIGHTS**

- In Zémio, insecurity is driving population movements towards Zapaï in DRC.
- More than 4,000 people affected by torrential rains are receiving cash assistance in Bangassou.
- In Am-Dafock, access to safe drinking water has improved for more than 11,500 internally displaced persons.

**GENERAL CONTEXT**

Haut-Mbomou Prefecture, South-East

- From 11 to 14 August, population movements were reported from Komboni, located about 5 km from Zémio, to Zapaï in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC). The movements followed military operations conducted against armed elements in the area. Persistent insecurity continues to affect livelihoods by restricting access to farmland and disrupting harvesting activities. As food security conditions deteriorate, some households have been forced to sell part of the essential household items received through humanitarian assistance to meet their immediate food needs.

**HUMANITARIAN NEEDS AND RESPONSE**

**Multi-sector**

Ouham-Fafa Prefecture, North-West

- From 15 to 20 August, COOPADEM strengthened the livelihoods of 45 members of local associations from both host communities and displaced populations at the Gbazara site in Batangafo. Beneficiaries received a community micro-grant and training on management and sustainable monitoring of income-generating activities to enhance their economic self-reliance. The initiative also aims to strengthen beneficiaries’ participation in youth-led community mobilization and awareness-raising activities, particularly on social cohesion and protection of internally displaced persons (IDPs), thereby contributing to more inclusive governance of displacement sites and host communities. In parallel, soap-making activities enabled women to develop livelihood opportunities while improving the living conditions of vulnerable households. These activities were implemented with financial support from the Central African Republic Humanitarian Fund (CAR HF).

**Food Security**

Vakaga Prefecture, North-East

- From 11 to 14 August, Triangle Génération Humanitaire (TGH) provided cash assistance to 22 agricultural groups in Birao. The intervention benefited 1,000 households from host communities and returnee populations. Beneficiaries also received training on fodder crop production techniques to strengthen their livelihoods and enhance their agricultural production capacity.

**CONTEXTE GÉNÉRAL**

Préfecture du Haut-Mbomou – Sud-Est

- Du 11 au 14 août, des mouvements de population ont été rapportés depuis le village de Komboni, situé à environ 5 km de Zémio, vers la localité de Zapaï, en République démocratique du Congo (RDC). Ces déplacements font suite à des opérations militaires menées contre des éléments armés dans la zone. L’insécurité persistante continue également d’affecter les moyens de subsistance des populations, en limitant leur accès aux champs et en compromettant les activités de récolte. Face à la détérioration de leur situation alimentaire, certains ménages sont contraints de vendre une partie des articles ménagers essentiels reçus dans le cadre de l’assistance humanitaire afin de couvrir leurs besoins alimentaires immédiats.

**BESOINS ET RÉPONSE HUMANITAIRE**

**Multisectoriel**

Préfecture de l’Ouham-Fafa – Nord-Ouest

- Du 15 au 20 août, l’ONG COOPADEM a renforcé les moyens de subsistance de 45 membres d'associations locales issus des communautés hôtes et des personnes déplacées du site de Gbazara, à Batangafo. Les bénéficiaires ont reçu une micro-subvention communautaire ainsi qu'une formation sur la gestion et le suivi durable des activités génératrices de revenus (AGR), afin d'améliorer leur autonomie économique. Cette initiative vise également à renforcer leur participation aux actions de mobilisation communautaire et de sensibilisation menées par les jeunes, notamment sur la cohésion sociale et la protection des personnes déplacées, contribuant ainsi à une gouvernance plus inclusive des sites et des communautés d'accueil. En parallèle, des activités de saponification ont permis à des femmes de développer des moyens de subsistance tout en améliorant les conditions de vie des ménages vulnérables. Ces activités ont été mises en œuvre grâce au soutien financier du Fonds humanitaire pour la République centrafricaine (FH RCA).

**Sécurité alimentaire**

Préfecture de la Vakaga – Nord-Est

- Du 11 au 14 août, l’ONG Triangle Génération Humanitaire (TGH) a fourni une assistance en espèces à 22 groupements agricoles à Birao. Cette intervention a bénéficié à 1 000 ménages issus de la communauté hôte et des retournés. Les bénéficiaires ont également reçu une formation sur les techniques de production de plantes fourragères afin de renforcer leurs moyens de subsistance et leurs capacités de production.

fields.title: Nearly two children a day orphaned in DR Congo’s latest Ebola outbreak – Save the Children
fields.body:
**KINSHASA, 21 August 2026** – At least 180 children have lost both parents or primary caregivers in the Democratic Republic of Congo's (DRC) Ebola outbreak, equivalent to nearly two children every day, since the deadly virus was declared 100 days ago, Save the Children said.

Thousands more children have lost one parent or caregiver, exposing them to heightened risks of abuse, exploitation, trafficking and severe psychological distress as families and already fragile social services struggle to cope \[1\].

In what has become DRC’s deadliest ever outbreak, children are bearing some of most devastating and lasting consequences, including the loss of parents and caregivers and increased risks of abuse, exploitation and psychological distress.

Latest figures from the Provincial Division of Social Affairs in Ituri, the epicentre of the outbreak, show that 180 children - 90 boys and 90 girls - have lost both parents to the virus that was declared on 15 May. Most are now being cared for by relatives or in state-run childcare facilities while longer-term family-based arrangements are found.

A further 114 children, including 61 boys and 53 girls, are currently separated from their parents, and are being supported by humanitarian organisations and family members, while their parents receive treatment for Ebola.

Children who are orphaned, separated or left unaccompanied by Ebola face heightened risks of human trafficking, sexual exploitation, physical violence, forced recruitment by armed groups and severe emotional distress. In communities affected by the virus, children can also face stigma and isolation, while strained protection systems leave many without the care and support they urgently need.

According to [latest data from the Ministry of Health](https://insp.cd/sitrep-n093-mvebdb-15-08-2026/), over 4,945 cases of Ebola and 2,325 deaths have been reported to date. At least 800 children are confirmed to have contracted the disease with more than 357 children dying, accounting for nearly 32% of total confirmed deaths (1124) as of August 5 –the last available age-[disaggregated data from the Ministry of Health](https://insp.cd/sitrep-n083-mve-b_05-08-2026/). The true number is likely to be higher, Save the Children said.

The outbreak has expanded rapidly over the past 100 days. According to the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (Africa CDC), it has recorded around nine times more confirmed cases and six times more deaths than were reported during the same period of the 2014-2016 West Africa Ebola epidemic, the deadliest Ebola outbreak on record.

With the outbreak still spreading – now in six provinces up from just two – Africa CDC estimates that only about 10% of potentially exposed contacts have been identified, while about four in five new infections being found outside known chains of transmission, highlighting the scale of undetected spread.

Three out of every four deaths are occurring in the community rather than in health facilities, suggesting people are not accessing treatment in time. An investigation reported by [Science](https://www.science.org/content/article/exclusive-congo-s-ebola-epidemic-started-least-4-months-it-was-detected) also suggests Ebola may have been spreading around Mongbwalu in Ituri province as early as January - at least four months before the outbreak was officially declared.

Save the Children is working with government and partners in Ituri province to establish safe spaces – called Observation Care Centres - for children whose parents or caregivers are currently being treated for Ebola and don’t have alternative family care arrangements. These spaces will host children on a full‑time basis while their parents receive care in the Ebola Treatment Centre located in the same compound. Throughout a 21‑day surveillance period, the children will sleep, eat, live, and be supported psychologically in a safe environment.

**Emmanuel Kalinde, Child Protection Manager in Ituri, said:**

*"Behind every statistic is a child whose world has been turned upside down. Many of these children are mourning parents, grandparents, siblings and caregivers who were the centre of their lives. Grief can leave a child incredibly vulnerable, especially in communities already facing conflict and displacement. Our job is to help ensure that no child is left behind. With the right support they can begin to heal and regain a sense of hope."*

**Greg Ramm, Save the Children’s Country Director in the DRC, said:**

*"Ebola is stealing more than lives. It is taking away the people children run to when they are scared. Every child who loses a parent, caregiver or loved one faces a future filled with uncertainty, and many are at risk of being left without the protection and support they need.*

*“The children at the centre of this crisis need more than emergency medical care. They need safe care arrangements, protection, emotional support and the chance to continue learning and simply be children again. The longer this outbreak continues, the greater the risk that vulnerable children fall through the cracks and face exploitation, abuse, neglect or permanent disruption to their futures.*

*“Child protection cannot be treated as a secondary concern in an Ebola response. Every effort to stop transmission must be matched by efforts to protect the children left behind. Governments, donors and the international community must urgently invest in scaling up support for frontline health services, alternative care, mental health support, community-based child protection programmes, and the essential services families rely on.”*

This outbreak is unfolding in communities already affected by armed conflict, mass displacement and chronic humanitarian needs. For many children, Ebola is the latest shock in a series of crises that have already disrupted their safety, education and wellbeing, placing additional strain on already fragile health, protection and social support system.

Save the Children is supporting infection prevention, community engagement, case detection and referral, and the continuity of essential services for children and families. The aid agency is also providing psychosocial support and child protection services, including support for children who have lost caregivers, while working to ensure children can continue learning and access healthcare, nutrition and protection services safely throughout the crisis.

In the DRC since 1994, Save the Children partners with 13 local organisations, as well as international agencies and government authorities, to deliver life-saving support in health, nutrition, education, child protection, food security, water, sanitation, and hygiene for children and their families.

**ENDS.**

**Notes to editors**

\[1\] Over 2,000 people have died from Ebola, according to [latest data from the Ministry of Health](https://insp.cd/sitrep-n093-mvebdb-15-08-2026/), most of them adults and parents to many children and thus thousands of children have lost a parent or caregiver.

fields.title: How Caritas is supporting communities affected by Ebola in the DRC
fields.body:
Three months after the Democratic Republic of the Congo declared its 17th Ebola outbreak on 15 May 2026, the situation remains deeply concerning. The outbreak continues to spread in the east of the country, driven by the rare Bundibugyo strain, for which there is currently no licensed vaccine or approved treatment.

The World Health Organization is currently assessing whether existing Ebola vaccines and available treatments could be effective against this strain.

As of mid-August 2026, **authorities have recorded 4,945 confirmed cases and 2,325 deaths** — a case fatality rate of 46 per cent — across six provinces: Ituri, North Kivu, South Kivu, Haut-Uélé, Tshopo and Bas-Uélé. Declared on 15 May, the outbreak passed 1,000 confirmed cases within 40 days, making it the fastest-growing Ebola epidemic on record.

Caritas Congo ASBL is working through its diocesan networks, parishes and community health structures to support affected families, promote prevention and strengthen the response.

Drawing on long-standing relationships with local communities, Caritas teams are helping to build trust, share reliable information and ensure that people affected by the outbreak are not left alone. Abbé Edouard Makimba Milambo, Executive Secretary of Caritas Congo ASBL, recently spoke to the news outlet *Crux*. Below is a summary of the interview.

## **The United Nations has described this outbreak as the largest and fastest-spreading ever recorded, caused by the Bundibugyo strain of the Ebola virus. From Caritas’ perspective in eastern DRC, does that description match the reality on the ground?**

Yes, unfortunately, that description matches what Caritas teams are observing alongside the diocesan Caritas structures concerned. Behind the figures are families living in anguish, villages whose habits have been turned upside down, and health workers operating under intense pressure.

The epidemic is progressing rapidly, cases are touching several health zones, and local capacities are already stretched thin. In eastern DRC, population displacement, insecurity, mobility linked to mining activity and the fragility of the health system are making the outbreak considerably harder to control. For Caritas Congo ASBL, this situation represents a health emergency, a social crisis and a major challenge for communities, all at once.

## **What impact is this epidemic having on people’s daily lives and on the health system?**

The impact is profound and is felt in households’ everyday lives. Families live with the fear of the disease, of losing a loved one, or of prolonged isolation. Markets are running at a slower pace, some small traders are seeing their custom shrink, and day labourers can lose their main source of income. In the most vulnerable households, that loss of income quickly translates into food insecurity.

Health centres, already short of staff, equipment and medicines, must strengthen infection prevention and control measures while still delivering essential care.

> “One of the most worrying consequences is that some people are delaying seeking care for fear of being identified as suspected cases.”

## **Can you share an example or a testimony from a member of your team that illustrates what affected families are currently going through?**

An example that comes up often in our exchanges with local teams in the affected dioceses is that of families struck by several bereavements within a few days, while also having to cope with isolation, fear from their neighbours, and uncertainty about tomorrow.

> “We are told of parents who can no longer hold their children in their arms during treatment or follow-up, of children who do not understand why a relative has been taken away, and of families who must accept dignified and safe burial measures even as they are living through immense grief.”

These measures are not rejected because families refuse to protect the community; they are sometimes difficult to accept because they touch on very sensitive cultural, spiritual and family practices. That is where our pastoral, social and community presence takes on its full meaning: listening, explaining, accompanying, and helping families feel that they are not alone.

## **How do you convince terrified populations to trust medical interventions?**

Caritas’s strength lies in being present alongside communities well before crises hit. Through parishes, diocesan structures, community outreach workers and faith-based health centres, we often share in people’s daily lives.

> “In practical terms, we take the time to listen to concerns, to answer questions in local languages, and to work with people the community trusts: priests, religious sisters and brothers, community leaders, women leaders, young people and survivors. When a message is carried by someone the community knows and respects, it is better understood and better accepted.”

Trust is built when families understand that the measures being proposed are meant to protect them, preserve their dignity and save lives.

## **As traditional donors scale back their support, who is financing the response to the epidemic today?**

At this stage, the response is being coordinated by the DRC government, with support from WHO, the United Nations system, the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (Africa CDC), and numerous technical, financial, humanitarian and faith-based partners. Within the Caritas Internationalis network, organisations such as Caritas International Belgium, CRS, CAFOD, Caritas Germany, Secours Catholique-Caritas France, Caritas Spain, Caritas Italiana and Caritas Austria are providing valuable financial, technical, institutional and humanitarian support.

Despite this backing, needs remain significant, particularly around community mobilisation, psychosocial support, local logistics, prevention and the long-term strengthening of health structures. At this stage, Caritas is observing above all a growing strain on local structures, which must respond to rising needs with limited means. We cannot say that health centres have closed purely because of budget cuts. What is clear, however, is that some essential activities can be slowed, delayed or placed under heavy pressure when funding is not available in time. That risks weakening the effectiveness of the response and making it harder to protect the most vulnerable populations.

Sustained resource mobilisation remains essential to guarantee an effective response and protect the most vulnerable populations.

## **What concrete actions is Caritas currently carrying out on the ground in eastern DRC to slow the virus’s spread and support affected communities?**

Caritas contributes mainly to community mobilisation, awareness-raising on prevention measures, the dissemination of reliable messages, referring suspected cases to the appropriate services, and supporting affected families. Concretely, that means going out to communities, engaging with local leaders, explaining warning signs, encouraging handwashing, supporting acceptance of contact tracing, accompanying bereaved families, and helping to reduce the stigmatisation of people who are infected or have recovered. Through its parish, diocesan and health networks, Caritas also helps build acceptance of medical interventions by showing that the response is not imposed on communities but built together with them. For Caritas Congo ASBL, hope rests on solidarity, trust and the conviction that every life saved is the result of a collective effort.

*The full interview by reporter Ngala Killian Chimtom, published on Crux, 7 August 2026, [is available at this link](https://cruxnow.com/interviews/2026/08/combating-fear-with-faith-how-caritas-is-fighting-drcs-fastest-spreading-ebola-outbreak).*

The post [How Caritas is supporting communities affected by Ebola in the DRC](https://www.caritas.org/article/how-caritas-is-supporting-communities-affected-by-ebola-in-the-drc/) appeared first on [Caritas](https://www.caritas.org).
